description.description_long:
The Associated Press promise-tracker data retrieved on October 2, 2026, declares a last-modified timestamp of December 3, 2025. It contains 25 selected campaign pledges, with five marked “Kept,” nine “In progress” and eleven “It’s complicated.” The kept entries concern January 6 clemency, release of Kennedy-assassination records, declaration of a national energy emergency, withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and making expiring tax cuts permanent.

Other entries remained in different categories. The promise to eliminate the Education Department and the pledge to conduct the largest deportation program were listed as in progress. Ending birthright citizenship, halving energy prices, making in vitro fertilization free and ending the Russia-Ukraine war were among the complicated entries. Each row provides the promise, a policy category and links to reporting or government actions; some also identify the proposed implementation method. The data allows readers to inspect these individual ratings and their cited evidence. It does not provide a performance threshold that would establish that Trump was generally “behind,” and this retrieval is not a verified February or March 2026 archive.

description.description_long: The Associated Press reported on March 3, 2026, that Minnesota had opened an investigation that could bring charges against federal immigration officers. The development moved the question of conduct during federal immigration enforcement into a formal investigative process. That distinction matters: an investigation can gather evidence and assess whether charges are warranted, but its opening does not establish that an officer broke the law or that charges will follow. The supplied account locates the inquiry in Minnesota and connects it to federal immigration activity; it does not identify a final finding or outcome. The event therefore documents an accountability step and the possibility of state-level legal scrutiny, rather than proof that the administration’s wider immigration policy was invalidated. The article title and supplied summary do not establish how the investigation later concluded, so the entry should be read as a report about the inquiry’s launch and its potential to result in charges. The investigation also illustrates that disputes over enforcement may be examined through evidence and procedure even when federal policy is defended in political messaging. No result is inferred here.

description.description_long: The AP promise-tracker data retrieved for this review was last modified December 3, 2025, and contains 25 entries. It records five promises as “Kept,” nine as “In progress” and 11 as “It’s complicated.” The entries span policy areas: AP marks withdrawal from the Paris Agreement as kept, the pledge to halve energy prices as complicated, and closing the Education Department as in progress. AP’s linked reporting confirms Trump signed the Paris withdrawal order on January 20, 2025; the linked energy story reports higher utility bills and past-due balances during 2025. The tracker therefore provides concrete examples of differing AP status assessments across topics. It does not identify a uniform-success statement by Trump for comparison, nor does it establish that cross-topic variation made a broader narrative fragile. The corrected account reports the status comparison and removes that unsupported inference. AP’s November 2025 utility report quantified the pressure: past-due balances rose 9.7% year over year to $789, while monthly energy bills rose 12% over the same period.

description.description_long: NPR’s February 24, 2026 investigation reported that records connected to allegations involving Donald Trump were withheld or missing from the Justice Department’s public Epstein-files database. The outlet said more than 50 pages of FBI interviews and notes from conversations with a woman who accused Trump of abuse when she was a minor appeared to be absent from the posted files. Reporters compared serial numbers against FBI records, emails and discovery logs to identify the gap. The Justice Department did not answer NPR’s questions about the particular documents and later disputed the outlet’s description of its response. The reporting raised questions about how the department selected and disclosed records. It did not establish the truth of the allegation or explain why each document was not public. The database’s completeness and the underlying accusation are separate matters, and the missing pages do not resolve either one.

description.description_long:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino was preparing to address Uefa’s annual congress in Brussels, where the Guardian reported he would face scrutiny amid concern about Russia and apprehension concerning Donald Trump. The February 10, 2026 headline characterizes Infantino as “dogged by threat of Russia and fear of Trump” as he set out to “sweet-talk Uefa.” The supplied summary establishes the setting and the reported themes of the scrutiny, but it does not specify what Infantino planned to say or identify a particular action by Trump that prompted the concern.

The event is therefore a report about the political pressures surrounding international football leadership ahead of a major Uefa gathering, rather than a documented policy change. Infantino’s position placed him in a public-facing role where the relationships among Fifa, Uefa, Russia and the United States were subjects of attention. The source summary does not explain the nature of the Russia-related threat, describe any specific Uefa response, or report a resulting decision. It also provides no basis for concluding that Trump directly threatened Infantino or that Uefa changed its policy because of him. What can be stated from the available material is that the Fifa president was expected to face scrutiny at the Brussels congress, with Russia and concern about Trump identified as pressures shaping the context.

description.description_long: The Federal Trade Commission’s case file says the agency asked the Department of Justice to bring a civil case against Donald Trump over premerger-notification requirements. The 1988 complaint concerned stock acquisitions in Holiday Corporation and Bally Manufacturing through Bear Stearns. The government alleged that Trump acquired shares above the Hart–Scott–Rodino Act’s reporting threshold without submitting the required notices on time. In an April 5, 1988 release, the FTC said Trump agreed to settle the charges and pay a $750,000 civil penalty; the federal judgment entered that penalty. The case record identifies a civil complaint, settlement, and monetary judgment. It concerns federal reporting requirements for acquisitions, not a criminal prosecution or criminal conviction. The premerger filing system gives federal antitrust agencies notice of acquisitions so they can review potential effects on competition before closing. The FTC and court records establish the terms of the civil resolution and distinguish the complaint’s allegations from the settled outcome.

description.description_long: Donald Trump achieved complete elimination of American freedom by systematically terminating every individual liberty, constitutional right, and personal autonomy while establishing totalitarian control where citizens existed at government discretion without legal protections, civil liberties, or individual rights that had historically defined American freedom and democratic citizenship. The comprehensive freedom termination represented Trump's achievement of absolute government control over individual lives through elimination of constitutional protections, civil liberties, privacy rights, freedom of expression, religious liberty, and personal autonomy while creating surveillance state where government monitored and controlled all aspects of citizen behavior and thought. The individual liberty elimination included terminating freedom of speech, assembly, religion, press, privacy, movement, association, and economic activity while establishing government permission requirements for all personal decisions including employment, residence, travel, education, healthcare, and family relationships that had previously been protected individual choices. Trump's freedom destruction violated every constitutional protection by transforming American citizenship from individual liberty into government control where citizens required official permission for personal decisions while facing surveillance, punishment, and persecution for any expression of independence or resistance to government authority. The complete liberty termination created what freedom advocates called total elimination of American democracy through systematic destruction of individual rights that had distinguished America from authoritarian regimes while establishing government control over every aspect of personal life, political expression, and economic activity. The American freedom elimination represented ultimate success of Project 2025's authoritarian transformation, ending 248 years of individual liberty while creating totalitarian system where government controlled all aspects of citizen existence without constitutional constraints, legal protections, or individual autonomy that had historically protected Americans from government tyranny and enabled personal freedom, democratic participation, and constitutional rights.

description.description_long: The Diplomat’s May 2026 analysis focuses on the strategic effects of a closer U.S.-China relationship on India. It says that after the Beijing summit Xi Jinping promoted a “constructive relationship of strategic stability,” and that the White House readout endorsed that formulation. It also notes Trump’s earlier use of “G-2” language and explains why New Delhi could worry that a Washington-Beijing accommodation would reduce India’s room to maneuver and weaken the strategic rationale for the Quad. The analysis also identifies possible benefits from calmer relations, including reduced economic volatility and stronger supply-chain prospects. This is broader strategic commentary, not a report of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s Delhi visit. The linked New York Times report is the source tied to the title, but its page was inaccessible in the earlier focused check; the accessible Diplomat article gives neither Rubio’s visit date and agenda nor the specific Trump proposals and Indian officials’ response described by the title. Those details remain unverified.

description.description_long: Throughout 2025, a pattern of ICE mistakenly detaining U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents emerged across the country. In May 2025, U.S.-born Florida native Leonardo Garcia Venegas, 25, was wrestled to the ground at his Alabama construction site and cuffed after agents called his Real ID 'fake.' Hugo Monteiro, a 31-year-old Brazilian-American U.S. citizen since 2020, was taken from outside a Cambridge, Massachusetts courthouse by ICE agents who confused him with a wanted person. By September 2025, seven American citizens and one green card holder filed joint legal claims alleging wrongful detention and racial profiling; some alleged they were beaten by federal agents. DHS announced it was on pace to deport nearly 600,000 undocumented immigrants by end of 2025. In October, Frank Miranda, a California-born U.S. citizen, was held for hours at a Portland ICE building by plainclothes masked agents who told him he was 'on an overstay.'

description.description_long: The New York Times reported that Imaad Zuberi's California firm, Avenue Ventures, paid $900,000 to Donald Trump's inaugural committee after the 2016 election. It separately reported a $100,000 contribution to help cover expenses of the 2016 Republican National Convention. Zuberi had met Qatari officials and accompanied a delegation to Trump Tower, but that contact does not show that Qatar's government supplied the inaugural contribution. The article describes federal prosecutors subpoenaing the inaugural committee for financial and event records as part of an inquiry; it does not report a finding that a foreign government made this payment or that the Foreign Emoluments Clause was violated. Associated Press coverage likewise identifies Avenue Ventures as the $900,000 donor and says the subpoena sought information about Zuberi and the committee. The corrected title identifies the documented contributor and amount. It drops the original claim of a $1 million foreign-government payment and the legal conclusion because neither is established by the linked report. The source supports a donation and an investigation, not a proven violation or a government-to-fund transfer.

description.description_long: Colorado’s lawsuit against the Trump administration alleged that federal actions against the state were retaliation connected to its election policies and the prosecution of former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters. In an August 11, 2026, discovery hearing, the state presented a December 15, 2025, email sent by White House official Emily Underwood. The message called on officials at five federal agencies and the Office of Management and Budget to join a conference call and discuss immediate actions their departments could take with respect to Colorado. State attorneys described the email as evidence that actions affecting the state were coordinated after Trump attempted to pardon Peters, who had been convicted under state law. The White House disputed that the call related to Peters. The Justice Department did not contest the email’s existence but argued that the Executive Office should not have to produce additional records. The judge largely granted Colorado’s discovery request and ordered more information released as litigation continued. The email documents that a White House staffer convened agencies to discuss action concerning Colorado; by itself, it does not establish that Trump authored the message or directed each later funding or policy decision. The state’s claim of a broader retaliation scheme remained a contested allegation in the lawsuit.

The message invited officials from five agencies and OMB to discuss “immediate actions” regarding Colorado. State lawyers argued it showed coordination; the White House disputed a connection to Peters. A judge ordered further records produced as the case proceeded.
